title: The Rumor Against Krishna
story:
The Syamantaka had been in Dwaraka only a few seasons, and already everyone in the city knew whose neck it hung on. The jewel — a gift of the sun god — was said to fill its owner's coffers with gold, to bring rain in its season, to keep disease from the house that held it. It had come to rest around the neck of Satrajit, a noble of the Yadu clan, who walked through Dwaraka glowing like a second sun.

Krishna asked for the jewel. He did not demand it, though he could have taken it; he did not scheme for it; he simply asked. Satrajit refused. He was a greedy man, and the Syamantaka was the finest thing he had ever owned; he could not bear to part with it. Krishna let the matter rest. But the refusal did not rest. It lodged in the city's memory, and in Dwaraka, where everyone watched everyone else, a memory like that had a way of growing teeth.

Then Prasena went hunting. Prasena was Satrajit's brother, and one morning he rode out into the forest wearing the Syamantaka at his throat. He did not ride back. A lion had brought him down — killed him and his horse together — and then the lion itself had been struck dead in turn, by a great bear, who took the jewel from the kill and carried it into the mountains.

When the news reached Dwaraka, no one spoke of lions or bears. The city remembered that Krishna had asked for the Syamantaka and been refused, and a whisper began to move through the streets like wind through standing grain: Krishna had killed Prasena. He had wanted the jewel; now Prasena was dead and the jewel was gone; who else could have done it? The whisper grew, and every retelling sharpened it.

Krishna heard what the city was saying. He did not rage, and he did not answer with speeches. He knew he was innocent, and he knew that words would not prove it — only the jewel would. "I must bring the jewel back," he said, and with his followers he set out for the forest where Prasena had gone.

The trail was written plainly on the earth for anyone who knew how to read it. Krishna followed the tracks of horse and rider through the forest, up into the Rikshavan mountains and across the flanks of the Vindhya ranges, searching every path and hollow until weariness began to pull at his limbs. Then he found Prasena — Prasena and his horse, both dead in a clearing, and no jewel on either. Near them lay the lion, killed by something greater than itself. The footprints around the kill told the rest of the story: a bear had taken the jewel from the lion's body and carried it away.

Krishna followed the bear's trail to the mouth of a den in the mountainside — a vast, dark opening that breathed cold air. From inside came a woman's voice, low and coaxing, the way a nurse speaks to a child. She was playing with the jewel, offering it to a little one. "Do not weep," she was saying. "The lion killed Prasena, and the lion was killed by Jambavan. So do not weep, my good boy — this Syamantaka belongs to you."

There it was. No one in Dwaraka had spoken a word in Krishna's defense, but the den had just cleared his name: the bear king Jambavan had taken the jewel from the lion, and the jewel now lay in the hands of Jambavan's own cub, kept as a plaything.

Krishna left his elder brother Balarama and the Yadavas, the men of his own clan, at the mouth of the den. Then, alone and silent, his bow in his hand, he stepped into the darkness.
reflection: Krishna's answer to the rumor is not a defense but a search: he lets the truth travel the same ground the accusation did, from the city to the forest to the den, and it vindicates him without a single argument. The city was ready to believe the worst; the evidence was ready to prove otherwise.
next_story_tease: In the darkness of the den, the king of bears rose to meet him.
hero_scene: Krishna, alone at the mouth of Jambavan's vast dark den, stepping into the shadows with his bow in hand while Balarama and the Yadavas wait behind him at the entrance.
